results.content:
## Where Loom is the better choice

When you are the point. A code review, a bug report, feedback on a design. The viewer wants your voice and your reasoning, and an AI narrator would be worse.

One-off videos. Record, stop, paste the link. There is nothing to set up, and nothing to keep.

No repo, no agent. Loom needs a browser or its app. tday.com needs a coding agent on your machine and the app's code, except on Enterprise, where it can record in the cloud.

Conversation. Signed-in viewers can comment and react on the video, and Loom shows who watched.

## Where tday.com is the better choice

Demos that have to stay right. When the product changes, your agent records the demo again and it becomes a new version of the same demo. The share link and every docs embed play the new take. [...] ## Key takeaways

- Loom is a message. tday.com is documentation. You notice the difference the first time the UI changes.
- A Loom is recorded by a person, and recorded again by a person. A tday.com demo is recorded by your coding agent, and recorded again with one request.
- Loom carries your voice and face. tday.com voices each line with an AI voice and adds captions, camera moves and title cards.
- Loom is priced per user: $18 a month on Business, $24 with AI. tday.com is priced per plan: $39 a month on Pro, with 5 seats and 25 saved demos.
- Plenty of teams need both, because they answer different questions. [...] ## tday.com vs Loom at a glance

results.title: Loom alternatives for product demos (2026) | tday.com
results.content:
It is a better choice than Loom when a demo has to stay correct. A re-record becomes a new version of the same demo, so its share link and embeds play the new take. It is a worse one for most of what Loom is used for. Its narration is an AI voice unless you record yourself over it (tday.com writes the script, you read it off a teleprompter, and your camera take sits in the corner), it makes videos and not interactive tours, and it does not record on a push or a merge: you ask the agent each time. Free includes 5 saved demos and 100 credits a month, with a tday.com badge. Pro is $39 a month for 5 seats. More in tday.com vs Loom.

## When Loom is still the right tool [...] ## Demos a coding agent records

### tday.com

tday.com is the narrowest fit on this list. It only works for a team whose app runs from its repo on a developer's machine, with a coding agent such as Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. On Enterprise it can also record in the cloud. If nobody on the team works that way, skip it.

Where it fits, the agent does the recording: it starts a separate copy of the app with throwaway data and records one narrated line at a time. tday.com then voices each line with an AI voice and adds the cursor, camera moves, captions and title cards. A take can run up to 10 minutes. [...] A narrator. Loom carries your own voice. Its site lists AI voices and avatars as coming soon.

The free plan is small for demos too: 25 videos of up to 5 minutes each, at 720p, with no downloads.

Loom's pricing page on November 10, 2026, billed monthly: Starter $0, Business $18 and Business + AI $24 per user a month, and Enterprise.

results.title: tday.com: AI that turns your product into on-brand marketing content | Y Combinator
results.content:
There are two ways in, and both produce both outputs. Connect your repo and tday spins up an isolated sandbox, captures the exact change in each pull request before it even merges, and posts the assets back to the PR to review or auto-publish. Or hand us a demo account set up exactly how you want to be marketed, pick the feature, and tday signs in, drives the real flow, and records it.

What makes it different is that everything is grounded in your real product and brand. tday already knows your colors, fonts, and voice, so output is on-brand every time, and you can tweak any line, scene, or image from the platform without re-recording the source. Ship a new version and the demo re-records itself: it captures a capability, not a one-off moment. [...] It has never been quicker to build. Most companies are putting out new features or bug fixes daily. But do your users actually know what you shipped today?

Building has never been faster, but telling people about it hasn't kept up. Marketing what you shipped is slower than shipping it: record the demo, fumble fifteen takes, design the post, edit the video, get it on-brand, publish. An afternoon gone for twenty seconds of footage. So most teams skip it, and their best work ships to silence.

tday.com closes that gap. Connect your GitHub repo or point us at your site, and every release turns into a complete launch package: a demo video that shows how the feature works, a feature showcase built to sell it, and on-brand graphics for every placement, published to social automatically. [...] The creative we generate is already running at up to 8.3% CTR in early paid tests, several times the typical benchmark. Paid campaigns inside tday are next, and from there, marketing that scales at the speed you ship: hundreds of thousands of on-brand, hyper-targeted assets, generated and published automatically.
